lesson.grammar_point: quantifiers and numbers with the present perfect

listenings.text: Right, here are the numbers going into the final day. Our leader has entered all five events this season and she has qualified for four finals, which is the best record on the tour. Her average total is fourteen point one. Second place has a slightly lower average, thirteen point six, but she has won two events, so she has more big results and less consistency. The gap between them is two hundred and forty points, which sounds like a lot and is not. One good heat closes it. Heat win percentage: seventy per cent for the leader, sixty-two for second.

People ask me how many events a junior should do in a year, and the honest answer is fewer than they think. I have coached kids who have entered twelve events in a season and have not improved at all, because they have spent all their time travelling and no time training. Four or five is plenty. What matters is not how many events you have entered, it is how much time you have spent in the water between them. I would rather see an average of six point five and a lot of training than one big result and nothing else.

items.situation: Somebody asks how many competitions you have entered this year. Answer with a number.
Ask two questions about somebody's season: one with how many, one with how much.
Read this out loud as a sentence: 1st place 3,240 points, 2nd place 3,000.
Somebody asks if your season has been good. Use average and percentage.
Explain to a friend why one big result is not the same as a good season.

paras: A leaderboard looks simple and it is not. Five names, five totals, and a lot of information hidden between them.

The total is the number everybody looks at first: the two best waves of the heat, added together. A total of fifteen point four is very good. A total of nine is a bad morning. But the total on its own does not tell you much.

The average matters more over a season. If a surfer has entered five events and has an average of seven point two, that is a solid year, even if he has never won anything. Somebody with one big result and four bad ones has a lower average and a worse ranking.

Then there is the gap. If the gap between first and second is two points, the heat is basically finished. If the gap is three tenths, everybody on the beach is standing up. Commentators talk about the gap more than they talk about the scores, because that is where the story is.

And finally the percentage. Heat win percentage tells you how often somebody has got through to the next round. Sixty per cent is strong. It also means that four times out of ten, they have gone home early — which is the part nobody puts on the poster.
